title: Infra: GPU Fleet Capacity, Cloud Accounts & IaC CI/CD Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary

This playbook consolidates our current practices for managing the GPU fleet and capacity, required cloud accounts and networking configs, Terraform/IaC modules, and the CI/CD and build flows used to safely make infra changes. It is intended for on-call SREs, infra engineers, and platform owners responsible for capacity planning, deploys, and incident response.

Objectives
- Keep production GPU-backed model endpoints within latency and throughput SLOs while minimizing committed spend.
- Provide repeatable Terraform/IaC patterns and module usage to drive safe, reviewable changes.
- Standardize CI/CD validation and canary promotion for infra changes that affect capacity, networking, or billing.
- Provide clear runbook steps for common operational tasks and incidents.

Owners and Contacts
- Primary owner: Infra Engineering (owner: Aisha Patel)
- On-call escalation: infra-sre@redwood-inference.com, PagerDuty schedule: RID-INFRA
- CI/CD pipeline owner: Marco Chen
- Terraform module guardian: Rosa Martinez

High-level architecture assumptions
- GPU Fleet: multiple autoscaling pools partitioned by class (high-memory A100, general-purpose A10/A30, inference-optimized H100 variants in dedicated clusters).
- Control Plane: managed control plane services run in VPCs per environment (prod, staging, sandbox).
- Networking: VPC peering and Transit Gateway for cross-account connectivity; egress via NAT gateways in each availability zone.
- IaC: Terraform v1.5+ using our shared module registry (module versions pinned in environment manifests).
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions for plan/validate steps; a separate deploy runner in a secure management account performs applies with OIDC-based short-lived credentials.

Capacity & Utilization Policy
- Target GPU utilization: 55% average across each pool during peak windows (08:00-22:00 UTC).
- Buffer policy: maintain a 20% headroom over predicted peak to handle bursty traffic and model rollout spikes.
- Scale-up trigger: sustained 5-minute average GPU utilization > 70% for two consecutive 5-minute windows, or request queue length > 250 for 2 minutes.
- Scale-down trigger: sustained utilization < 40% for 15 minutes and queue length < 50.
- Spot vs Reserved mix: production pools should maintain at least 60% reserved capacity for critical models; non-critical batch pools can leverage spot with fallback policies.

Capacity Planning cadence
1. Weekly runway checks: infra team reviews 7-day usage, 14-day projected growth; update booking requests if runway < 21 days.
2. Monthly capacity review: align forecasts with product roadmap and upcoming model onboardings.
3. Quarterly commit decisions: recommend reserved instance commitments or cloud-savings plans based on 90-day usage projections.

Terraform / IaC modules: standards and patterns
- Module policy: all reusable modules must be in the infra-modules repo and include: README, variables.tf with descriptions, outputs.tf, examples/ directory, and an automated unit test (terratest or kitchen-terraform).
- Versioning: semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Consumers must pin module version in environment manifests; avoid using git "main" on production.
- Secrets: do NOT store secrets in Terraform state; use external KMS-backed secrets and reference them through data sources.
- State management: remote state in encrypted S3 buckets with DynamoDB locking. Separate state per environment and per logical area (networking, core infra, gpu-pools).
- Example module usage (environment manifest snippet):

  module "gpu_pool_prod" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//gpu-pool?ref=v1.3.0"
    pool_type = "a100-40gb"
    min_size = 2
    desired_size = 8
    max_size = 40
    reserved_capacity = 24
  }

CI/CD and validation flow
- Branch protection: all infra changes must be in a feature branch, go through PR with at least one module guardian review and one infra owner review.
- GitHub Actions pipeline steps (summary):
  1. lint (tflint, shellcheck)
  2. fmt check (terraform fmt -check)
  3. terraform init in a sandbox workspace (remote state mocked)
  4. terraform plan with var-file for target environment; post plan to PR as a comment
  5. unit tests (terratest) and policy checks (OPA/Conftest with policies in infra-policies repo)
  6. manual promotion step (approved by infra owner) for apply in staging
  7. apply in staging is run by deploy runner; smoke tests executed against staging
  8. automated canary apply in prod for low-risk changes (networking, IAM) or full deploy for capacity-only changes after approval

- Apply guardrails: requires a signed-off approvals file for changes that: modify networking, change reserved capacity > 10% of pool, or alter IAM roles. Applies over a certain cost delta (>$5k/month) require Finance review.

Networking and Cloud Accounts: essential configs
- Account structure: management account, prod account, staging account, sandbox account, and shared services account.
- VPC design: standard 3-AZ subnet topology per environment; control plane services in private subnets with NAT for outbound.
- DNS: hosted zones per environment with cross-account delegation for shared services.
- Security groups: least-privilege egress and ingress; all GPU fleet nodes communicate with control plane services over dedicated internal ports (8000-8010) and metrics/trace endpoints (9100, 9411).
- Cross-account role access: short-lived roles used by deploy runners; role bindings are auditable and rotated quarterly.

Runbooks: common operational procedures
1) Emergency scale-up (on-call)
- Symptoms: model endpoints show 95th p95 token latency > 2x baseline or request queue > 500.
- Immediate actions (pager):
  a. PagerDuty -> declare incident, assign SRE and infra lead.
  b. Validate metrics: GPU utilization, queue length, pending launches in cloud provider console.
  c. If autoscaler not keeping up: temporarily increase desired_size for the affected pool:
     - SSH into management runner (bastion) and run: 
       cd /opt/infra/deploys/envs/prod && gh workflow run gpu-scale-manual.yml -f pool=pool-name -f delta=+10
  d. Monitor new nodes until they register and model replicas rebalance.
  e. If nodes fail to come up, open cloud provider support ticket and escalate to platform engineering lead.

2) Terraform apply rollback (failed apply)
- If an apply fails mid-step and leaves partial resources:
  1. Do not re-run apply immediately. Notify the infra-owner on-call.
  2. Run terraform state list to identify partially created resources.
  3. Use terraform state rm <resource> for orphaned resources that can be recreated, or manually delete resources in cloud console if required.
  4. Re-run plan and apply in a controlled window.

3) Network change procedure (VPC/subnet or route table)
- High-level steps:
  1. Create change request and runbook; schedule maintenance window if change touches prod VPCs.
  2. Apply change first in sandbox -> staging; validate with smoke tests.
  3. For prod: create canary change in single AZ; validate service health for 30 minutes before full rollout.
  4. If degradation observed, roll back immediately using the previous Terraform state snapshot (we keep last 10 state snapshots).

Operational dashboards and alerts (recommended thresholds)
| Metric | Alert threshold | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pool GPU utilization (5m avg) | >80% | infra-sre | Pager at >90% |
| Request queue length | >300 | infra-sre | Trigger scale-up when sustained |
| Node boot failures (rate) | >5% over 10m | infra-platform | Investigate AMI or init script changes |
| Terraform plan drift | any drift | infra-engineering | Post as PR comment and block merge until resolved |

Testing and preflight checks
- All Terraform modules must pass unit tests and policy checks before merge.
- Integration smoke tests (lightweight) run in staging after apply: endpoint health, sample inference latency < threshold, and metrics ingestion verified.
- Nightly full-stack soak tests run against a dedicated staging cluster with synthetic traffic.

Audit, cost controls, and compliance
- Cost gating: PRs that increase committed spend by >$5,000/month are labeled "cost-impact" and require Finance approval.
- Audit logs: all control-plane API calls are logged to centralized logging (retention 365 days). Terraform applies must be associated with the GitHub actor and run-id for traceability.
- Secrets and keys: rotate deploy-role credentials quarterly; KMS keys used for state encryption must follow company key-rotation policy.

Maintenance & upgrade playbook
- AMI and GPU driver upgrades: test on staging nodes with a canary batch of 2 nodes and run the nightly soak before promoting to prod.
- Kernel/driver rollback: have images for last 3 known-good AMIs available and a documented rollback CLI command.
- Module upgrades: follow staged promotion: dev -> staging (smoke tests) -> prod (canary AZ) -> full promotion.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
- Force a planned scale-up (manual):
  gh workflow run gpu-scale-manual.yml -f pool=pool-name -f delta=+10
- Check Terraform remote state:
  aws s3 ls s3://redwood-terraform-state-prod/gpu-pools/
- Locking troubleshooting:
  aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name terraform-locks-prod
- Inspect recent apply run:
  gh run view <run-id> --repo redwood/infra-deploys

References
- infra-modules README: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-modules-ci-cd-guidelines-2026.json
- GPU capacity runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.json

This document should be reviewed at least quarterly or after any major platform change (new GPU class, new cloud provider region, or changes to reserved capacity strategy).
